title: Making soft goats' cheese at home
subtitle: A fresh, spreadable cheese from your own goats' milk in under 24 hours.
excerpt: Soft goats' cheese, known as chèvre in French dairies, is one of the simplest cheeses to make from fresh milk. It requires only a mesophilic starter culture and rennet, a few hours at room temperature, and draining overnight. The result is a soft, spreadable cheese with a clean, mild tang. Here is the method for a 1-litre batch using home milk.
sourceNotes: Home Cheese Making (Ricki Carroll, 2002), chèvre chapter. Neal's Yard Creamery, soft cheese method notes. Moorlands Cheesemakers, beginner soft cheese guide.

glossaryTerms.definition: A blend of lactic acid bacteria that works at moderate temperatures (20–30°C). Used in fresh cheeses, cream cheeses, and many semi-soft varieties. Produces lactic acid, which thickens the milk and begins curd formation.

An enzyme (chymosin) that cleaves the milk protein casein, causing it to form a gel. Available as liquid animal rennet, vegetarian microbial rennet, or fermentation-produced chymosin. A few drops are enough to set 1 litre of milk.

to set the curd over 12 to 18 hours at room temperature. The long, slow set produces a very fine, smooth curd that drains easily into a spreadable cheese. Speed it up and you get a grainy texture.
1 litre fresh goats' milk (pasteurised or raw; raw milk gives a more complex flavour)
1/8 teaspoon mesophilic starter culture (or the amount specified on the packet for 1 litre)
2 drops liquid rennet diluted in 2 tablespoons of cold, unchlorinated water
1/2 teaspoon fine salt (to taste, added at draining)
Warm the milk to 21 to 22°C in a clean, stainless or enamelled pan. Check with the cheese thermometer.

Sprinkle the starter culture over the surface of the milk. Leave for 2 minutes to rehydrate, then stir gently with a clean spoon for 30 seconds, using up-and-down strokes to distribute the culture through the full depth of the milk.
Add the diluted rennet and stir in the same way for another 30 seconds.
Cover the pan with a clean cloth and leave undisturbed at room temperature (20 to 22°C) for 12 to 18 hours. The curd should set firm enough to leave a clean break when you tilt the pan.
Line a colander with cheesecloth and ladle the curd in gently. Do not pour; pouring breaks the curd and you lose solids into the whey.

Tie the corners of the cloth and hang the bundle over a bowl in the fridge. Allow to drain for 8 to 12 hours until the cheese reaches your preferred texture. Shorter drain time gives a softer, more spreadable cheese; longer gives a firmer result.
Turn the cheese out, season with salt, and serve or refrigerate. Use within five days.

attrs.title: Yield from 1 litre of goats' milk

content.text: Expect 180 to 250 g of soft cheese from 1 litre of fresh goats' milk. Yield varies with fat content and the length of the drain. The remaining whey can be used in bread dough or fed to pigs.
